analysis.one_liner: Applies federal workplace laws—wages, safety, civil rights, family leave—to Congress and its own employees.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 28 Senate cosponsors to make Congress live under the workplace laws it imposes on everyone else got one hearing but never a vote, dying in committee as the 1994 Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Congress has long exempted its own offices from federal employment laws that apply to every other employer. This bill would apply core workplace protections—minimum wage and overtime, workplace safety, bans on discrimination by race, sex, age, and disability, and family and medical leave—to the roughly tens of thousands of people who work for Members, committees, and congressional agencies. It would create an Office of Compliance to handle complaints, from counseling and mediation up to a formal hearing and court review, and require periodic safety inspections of Capitol facilities. It also would open some legislative-branch offices to the Freedom of Information Act, though it carved out Member personal offices and committees.
analysis.who_benefits: Congressional employees—staffers in personal and committee offices, and workers at congressional agencies like the Architect of the Capitol, the Library of Congress, and the Government Printing Office—gain the right to sue or file complaints over unpaid overtime, unsafe conditions, discrimination, and denial of family leave. Disabled visitors gain enforceable accessibility rights in Capitol public spaces. The public gains some information rights over legislative-branch offices.

how_it_helps.text: Applies the Fair Labor Standards Act to congressional offices, giving employees minimum wage and overtime protections they previously lacked [S2][S3].
Extends bans on discrimination by race, sex, religion, national origin, age, and disability, plus the Family and Medical Leave Act, to congressional employment [S2][S3].

Creates an Office of Compliance with a step-by-step complaint process—counseling, mediation, a formal hearing before independent officers, and court review—and makes it illegal for a Member or supervisor to retaliate against an employee for using these rights [S2][S3].

Requires regular workplace-safety inspections of legislative facilities and requires the results to be published in the Congressional Record, and applies disability-access rules to Capitol public accommodations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and congressional employing offices would bear compliance costs, potential damages and settlements, and would lose the ability to fire or set conditions for staff without regard to the same rules other employers follow.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their offices

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts Member personal offices, committees, leadership offices, and caucuses from the Freedom of Information Act and Privacy Act, so the offices with the most politically sensitive information stay closed to the public [S2][S3].

It expressly allows party affiliation, domicile, and 'political compatibility' to be considered in firing personal, committee, and leadership staff—so most congressional employees would remain at-will on political grounds [S3].

Employees must go through counseling and mediation before filing a formal complaint, hearings are confidential, and the process rules out punitive damages, which would make many claims quieter and cheaper for offices to settle [S3].
Congress retains the power to veto the Office of Compliance's implementing regulations by concurrent resolution, keeping final control over how the rules apply to its own offices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For congressional employees, the bill would deliver real, enforceable rights they entirely lacked, even with the political-affiliation carve-out and the FOIA exemptions for Member offices. The costs fall almost entirely on Members and their offices—the very people who would have had to vote for it—and the design concessions in the bill appear aimed at making that easier. The main honest objection is that the multi-step confidential process is slower and weaker than the protections private-sector workers already have.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with 28 bipartisan cosponsors, referred to the Governmental Affairs Committee, got one hearing in June 1994—and then sat there until the Congress ended in January 1995, never reported out and never voted on.

narrative.text: Sen. Joseph Lieberman introduced the Congressional Accountability Act in the Senate on May 4, 1994, joined by original cosponsors including Republicans Charles Grassley and William Nickles and Democrats Barbara Boxer, Dianne Feinstein, and Barbara Mikulski [S1][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Governmental Affairs [S5].
The committee held hearings on June 29, 1994, but the bill was never reported out of committee and never received a Senate floor vote before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].
At the end, 28 senators—20 Democrats and 8 Republicans—had signed on as cosponsors, but that support never translated into floor action [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and their offices, who kept their exemption from the wage, overtime, safety, discrimination, and leave laws every other employer must follow. Congressional employees stayed without those rights.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress, who kept their exemptions

for.name: Sen. Joseph Lieberman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 28 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including original cosponsors Sen. Grassley (R-IA) and Sen. Nickles (R-OK).

against.name: Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. John Glenn (D-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, held hearings on June 29, 1994, and never reported it out; no floor vote ever occurred.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor in the months after its committee hearing, despite its bipartisan cosponsor list.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start—28 cosponsors split 20 Democrats and 8 Republicans—so the bill died without any vote that would have shown a party split.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and congressional employing offices
industries.note: As employers, Member offices, committees, and congressional agencies would face the wage, safety, discrimination, and leave obligations other employers already bear, plus potential liability for violations. They are the bill's regulated party and the group in a position to stop it.

Staff and workers at congressional agencies would gain enforceable overtime, safety, anti-discrimination, and family-leave rights for the first time, through an Office of Compliance complaint process.
